item.title: CMU Impression After ~20 Years
item.dc:creator: Ben
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

My son was attending Carnegie Mellon’s summer camp – alma mater for my wife and me – so we gave ourselves a “campus reunion” the day before! Familiar streets, familiar buildings, and so many fond memories – can’t believe it’s been 20 years already!

In particular we paid a visit to Newell Simon Hall – my old academic home! Guess who greeted us when we stepped right inside NSH? Valerie now has a new name: Tank! 😆 Twenty years on and it’s still here! Also took a picture of my old office 4611 and the NSH atrium, where we had so many TGIFs! It was a blast!

item.title: HM #89: Exploring Pittsburgh North Shore
item.dc:creator: Ben
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

This #LongRunSunday I ran my 89th HM on the Three Rivers Heritage Trail in Pittsburgh! An EZ 14.01mi at 9’46”/mi, EG 413ft with HR 131/143 and VO₂max 54.2. Consumed 2 gels, 8oz electrolyte and 4 salt tablets, ingesting every 4mi. Stopped frequently for photos, also got slightly lost a couple times!

In the past 3 days I officially exhausted the riverside trails at South Side and North Shore westbound — ran them all to the first points of closure. 36.54mi in 4 days, not bad!

Highlight of the run: a large group sitting on a locked down bridge to practice yoga, with a DJ truck blasting some kind of New Age music. I guess they really have too many bridges in Pittsburgh!

item.title: My First Pittsburgh Parkrun
item.dc:creator: Ben
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

After two days of running 15mi in Pittsburgh, I ran my first-ever Pittsburgh Parkrun today! Official time 24:28 with a bit more distance at 3.17mi, otherwise it’s my fastest 5k this year: time 23:50 pace 7’40”/mi (still way off from 21:05 last year)! Weather was not very hot but 90+% humid. Adding to the drama, there’s no bathroom! I guess that could’ve made me faster or slower? 😆

We had ~20 runners and the majority of them were first-timers! I took a photo with Pat and Will — the volunteers today. Pat was actually the OG of this Parkrun, which started a bit over a year ago. They definitely need more runners to join the fun!

item.title: First Run Back in Pittsburgh
item.dc:creator: Ben
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

First run back in Pittsburgh in ~20 years — 7 easy miles along the Monongahela on the South Side Trail. Lots has changed, but plenty still felt like home. Flew in on a redeye, went straight to work, then squeezed this in (with a 40-min pause at mile 2 to take an emergency meeting 😅). HR stayed solidly Z2 the whole way and my watch flashed VO₂max 54 — almost my all-time high (54.3)!

Can’t wait to run Saturday’s Parkrun in Pittsburgh!

item.title: Frontier LLMs Disagree on 67% of Real-World Fact-Checks
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Kosta Jordanov of Lenz Research presented 1,000 recent real-user claims to the five top frontier LLMs and asked each for a verdict, then measured how often they agreed. The claims are live fact-check requests submitted to Lenz, a fact-checking platform, rather than benchmark items with public answer keys.

Two things should temper that 67%. Calling these “fact-checks” is generous: three of the five models get no sources and answer from memory, and some claims are dated after those models’ training cutoffs, so on those they are guessing about events they never saw. I come back to both in my notes.

What the study reports:

  • Setup: 1,000 claims, none older than February 15, 2026, each normalized into a single neutral testable proposition anchored to its submission date. Five models are forced to pick one of four labels (True / Mostly True / Misleading / False) with no explanation and no Abstain option: three parametric (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3 Pro) and two retrieval-augmented (Gemini 3 Pro + Search, Sonar Pro from Perplexity). There is no LLM grader and no ground truth. Every number comes from direct label agreement across the five verdicts.
  • The main result: on 67% of claims (672 of 1,000) at least one model dissents from the majority, or no majority forms at all. Two or more models dissent on 45%, and 13% split with no majority. Only 33% are unanimous.
  • The pigeonhole floor: since exactly one of the four buckets can be correct, any split means at least one model is wrong. That puts a floor of ≥1 model wrong on 67% of claims, ≥2 wrong on 45%, and ≥3 wrong on the 13% with no majority. It bounds inconsistency from below, without identifying which model is wrong on any given claim.
  • Substantive vs calibration: 34% of claims have a gap of two or more buckets between the most-disagreeing pair, and 21% are polar (one model says True, another says False). Panel agreement, scored with Krippendorff’s α at the ordinal level, is 0.639, structured but well short of interchangeable.
  • Poles vs. middle: True and False majorities reach full unanimity 43–47% of the time, but Mostly True majorities reach it 0% of the time and Misleading only 5%. Of the 328 unanimous claims, 204 are True, 120 are False, 4 are Misleading, and 0 are Mostly True.
  • Per-model behavior: agreement with the majority of the other four ranges from 69% (Sonar Pro) to 81% (GPT-5.4). Verdict distributions differ by model. Gemini 3 Pro concentrates at the poles (54% True, 40% False, ~3% in each middle bucket), while Claude Opus 4.7 spreads more evenly. The highest-agreeing pair is Gemini 3 Pro and Gemini 3 Pro + Search at 75%, which share a base model, and three pairs tie at the 53% floor.
  • By domain: disagreement runs from 53% (History) to 77% (Legal), with substantive gaps most common in Finance, General, and Legal claims (~39–40%).
  • Why a fresh corpus: public fact-check sets like AVeriTeC and PolitiFact are years old and likely part of the training data, so disagreement on them confounds inference with memorization. These are recent real-user submissions never paired with a canonical verdict in any public set, spanning health, science, finance, history, tech, and legal questions rather than mostly US political claims.
  • Artifacts: a per-claim CSV, a hash-pinned PDF, a versioned archival URL (v1.0), and a Zenodo DOI. A companion study is planned that human-labels the same corpus so both the frontier panel and Lenz’s own verdicts can be scored against ground truth.

My Notes

  • No room to say “I don’t know”: the panel has to pick a verdict even when “I don’t know” is the right call, and that hurts most in the middle, where Mostly True and Misleading almost never reach unanimity. AbstentionBench shows that forcing an answer on unanswerable questions lowers quality, and AVeriTeC keeps Not Enough Evidence and Conflicting Evidence labels for exactly this reason. Part of the 67% reflects the rubric’s design rather than model error.

  • Even the models that search disagree: the easy dismissal is that three of the five (GPT-5.4, Opus 4.7, Gemini 3 Pro) run on memory alone, so their splits just reflect what each happened to memorize. But take only the two that search the web, Gemini 3 Pro + Search and Sonar Pro: they still give different labels on 42% of claims. Most of that is one step apart, True versus Mostly True. On 6% they go fully opposite, one True and one False, down from 21% across all five. Both can pull the same sources, so that 6% comes down to the sources and how each model reads them.

  • The four labels aren’t clean: the pigeonhole floor only holds if exactly one label can be right, but the buckets aren’t clean. Misleading shades into both True and False, there’s no Mostly False, and “All almonds are grown in the U.S. state of California” is fairly called either False or Misleading. When two labels both fit, a split is two defensible reads of the same claim, which makes the “someone is wrong on 67%” floor softer than it sounds.

  • The data is open: the per-claim CSV lists every claim with all five model verdicts, so any agreement number here can be recomputed, including the 42% and 6% above. It has the verdicts but no ground truth, so nothing in it settles who is actually correct, only how much the models diverge.

  • What would actually settle this: let each model think out loud before it gives a label, and ask each one the same claim several times to see whether it even agrees with itself. A single forced pick can’t separate a genuinely contested claim from a model that happened to be inconsistent that run. The human-labeled pass over the same 1,000 claims, which the author has planned, will finally say who was right.

Related Posts

  • AVeriTeC: A Dataset for Real-world Claim Verification with Evidence from the Web: the human-annotated fact-check benchmark this study cites as its agreement ceiling (κ=0.619), with a richer verdict set that the four-bucket rubric here deliberately omits.
  • AbstentionBench: Reasoning LLMs Fail on Unanswerable Questions: direct support for the concern that forcing a verdict with no Abstain option degrades quality on exactly the contested claims where the panel splits.
  • Domain-Level Metacognitive Monitoring in Frontier LLMs: A 33-Model Atlas: another case of frontier behavior varying stably by domain, matching the History-to-Legal spread in disagreement here.
  • Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know: the calibration counterpoint, where a single model can often judge its own correctness even as a panel of five cannot agree on a verdict.

item.title: Teaching a Script to Draw a Map of My Runs
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

I have a little side project. Every run I do gets pulled into a local database that stitches together a few sources: the activity itself from Strava, plus readiness and recovery data from Apple Health and my watch’s FIT files. A script then draws a map of the route that ends up in my CoachClaude coaching notes. It started as a red squiggle on a stock basemap. Over about ten days of tinkering it turned into something I actually read: effort, landmarks, PRs, and even which direction I ran each stretch, all on one picture.

Because every version regenerates over the whole history, I can re-draw any past run with any version of the code. So here are the same two runs at each stage.

I picked two runs on purpose:

  • My Juneteenth half marathon (13.8 mi down the Seattle waterfront), a point-to-point with lots of named landmarks and several PRs (personal records). A good test of the labels and callouts.
  • The Bridle Trails 50K (29.5 mi of looping horse trails), where I ran a lot of the same singletrack more than once. That turns out to be the hard case that motivated the very last change.

Stage 1: a line on a map

The first version draws the route as a flat red line over an off-the-shelf OpenStreetMap tile, with start and finish markers. That’s it.

The half marathon is framed loosely, with a lot of open water and eastside street grid the run never touches, and the basemap piles on dashed ferry lanes, freeway shields, and tiny labels. It’s a map with my run on it, not a map of my run.

Stage 2: frame it tight, and mark the PRs

Two changes here. First, the map now zooms to fit the route and swaps the raw OpenStreetMap tiles for CARTO’s cleaner Voyager basemap, rendered at retina resolution so the labels stay crisp. They’re still CARTO’s labels, but there’s far less clutter to fight. Second, and the actual reason for this version, it pulls my Strava PRs and segment splits and drops little pills on the map (PR, ½mi·1K) right where they happened. The direction arrows got clearer too, so on the 50K you can now follow the flow of the loop.

Marking a personal best is the first bit of story added to the bare route. And tight framing means each run fills its own frame.

Stage 3: draw my own labels

Next I dropped the pre-labeled basemap entirely and started drawing the place names myself over a blank canvas: italic water names (Elliott Bay, Puget Sound, Fauntleroy Cove), neighborhood names, the parks the route runs through (Alki Beach Park, Me-Kwa-Mooks Park, Lincoln Park), and small brown triangles for nearby landmarks. On the 50K the street grid and green space come in as gentle context instead of clutter.

With someone else’s labels I couldn’t control what showed up or how loud it was. I’d get a gas station named but not the park I ran through. Drawing them myself means the map emphasizes what’s on my route, at a density I choose.

Stage 4: color the line by heart rate

Now the route line is no longer one color. It runs on a gradient from green (easy) through yellow to red (hard), driven by my heart-rate zones, with a new legend in the corner to read it by.

The map now shows effort in place. On the Juneteenth half you can see it’s almost all calm green, a controlled aerobic day, with only a couple of warmer patches near the end. On the 50K the difference between the runnable flats (green) and the grinding hills (orange and red) jumps right out.

Stage 5: call out the extremes

Here I added off-route callout pills for the per-run extremes: a brown ▲ pill at the peak-elevation point and a red ♥ pill at max heart rate, each with a thin leader line pointing to exactly where on the course it happened. The PR pills from stage 2 are still there.

The heart-rate gradient tells you roughly where it got hard. These pins tell you exactly where the hardest single moment was and what it cost. On the 50K the ♥ 183 is out on the east side.

Stage 6: split the retraced sections into lanes

The last change (for now): where I ran the same ground more than once (an out-and-back, a lap, a figure-8), the map now draws each pass as its own parallel lane beside the other, instead of one pass painting over the earlier one.

This is barely visible on the half but changes the 50K completely. The Juneteenth run almost never retraces itself, so it looks about the same as stage 5, which is exactly why I show both. But the 50K is full of repeated singletrack. In every earlier version, the last time I ran a trail simply painted over every earlier time, so a stretch I ran three times looked identical to one I ran once, and the effort colors from the earlier passes were hidden under the last. Now those sections read as thin loops with two colored lanes side by side, each keeping its own effort color and its own direction arrow. You can finally see that it was a lapped course, and how my effort on the same trail changed between passes.

Where it ended up

None of the underlying GPS changed across the six versions, only how much of the run the map shows.

There’s plenty left to do (shade, weather, surface type), but I like that I can point the newest version at a run from months ago and see it fresh. Onward.

Related Posts

  • CoachClaude Is Coming Up Nicely — the running-coach project these maps feed into.
  • A Juneteenth Run to Lincoln Park — the half marathon in the left column of every map above.
  • Bridle Trails 50K: Hot Cocoa, Sprained Ankle, No Horseshit — the looping trail 50K that motivated the lane-split rendering.
  • A Rube Goldberg Pipeline for Sharing Links — another walk through the personal tooling behind this blog.

item.title: Freeing the Law with LOCUS: A Local Ordinance Corpus for the United States
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Freeing the Law with LOCUS: A Local Ordinance Corpus for the United States [1] (arXiv preprint, June 2026), Denis Peskoff, Christopher Vu, and Diag Davenport (UC Berkeley), with independent researcher Joe Barrow, build a national, machine-readable corpus of U.S. local ordinances and a county-level access layer over them.

Progress in legal AI increasingly depends on access to authoritative legal text at scale. Yet one of the most consequential layers of American law remains largely absent from existing machine-readable corpora: local ordinances. Local codes govern zoning, housing, business licensing, public health, noise, animal control, and many other domains of everyday regulation, but they are fragmented across vendor platforms designed for human browsing rather than bulk research access. We introduce LOCUS—the Local Ordinance Corpus for the United States—a comprehensive corpus and county-harmonized access layer for U.S. municipal and county ordinance codes. The raw corpus, available for release to researchers, represents nearly all publicly available municipal and county ordinance codes. The resulting raw corpus contains codes from 9,239 cities and counties. A smaller county-harmonized LOCUS access layer provides coverage for the largest 2,309 of 3,144 U.S. counties, accounting for a majority of the population. We use OCR to handle the myriad of document formats that have kept the law from being a public resource. We release the corpus with coverage metadata to support reproducibility, downstream legal AI research, and the incremental expansion of machine-readable access to local law. We train a collection of ModernBERT-based classifiers and scorers to facilitate analyzing U.S. local law among several dimensions, such as opacity and paternalism, that have not previously been studied at this scale. LOCUS-v1 and its derivative models are available at: https://huggingface.co/datasets/LocalLaws/LOCUS-v1

Methods

LOCUS is built by a five-stage pipeline that turns scanned municipal codes into individually labeled and scored laws:

  • Collect. Browser automation plus vendor-specific download logic pull municipal and county codes from the commercial platforms that host them. The raw corpus is 9,239 valid PDFs, roughly 80 GB and about 7 million pages. Server-side assembly limits, anti-bot measures, 15-second crawl delays, and non-unique municipality names each needed targeted recovery rather than one generic scraper.
  • OCR. Every page image is converted to Markdown with LightOnOCR-2-1B [2], an open 1-billion-parameter vision-language model. Running on batch inference, OCR costs about $0.30 per 1,000 pages.
  • Segment. Post-processing strips repeated headers, footers, and page numbers, merges paragraphs and tables that cross pages, and splits the joined text into individual laws by section and subsection headers.
  • Classify. Three ModernBERT classifiers label each law for substantivity (does it state a rule, or is it structural or procedural?), function (rules, enforcement, structural, context, process), and topic (buildings, business, zoning, nuisance, other). The labels come from 100,000 laws annotated by GPT-5.4-nano, split 80,000 / 10,000 / 10,000 for training, tuning, and test.
  • Score. Each law is also placed on four continuous normative dimensions: enforcement discretion, opacity, paternalism, and problem salience.

The scoring stage is the most involved part of the method. Rather than ask a model for a number, the authors run 200,000 pairwise match-ups per dimension with GPT-5.4-nano, asking which of two ordinances better exemplifies the dimension, and judging every pair in both orders to cancel position bias. Each ordinance’s win-loss history is fed to TrueSkill [3], the Bayesian rating system Microsoft built for matchmaking, to recover a latent score. Those TrueSkill scores then become regression targets for a ModernBERT scorer, so the expensive pairwise judging happens once and the cheap encoder scores all 2.2 million laws.

Results

The released corpus is 2,211,516 text chunks, most judged substantive (stating rules or enforcement rather than structure or process). The classifiers are evaluated on a held-out 10,000-law test set. The four dimensional scorers are evaluated by Pearson correlation against the TrueSkill targets on a separate 1,000-ordinance test set per dimension. The macro analysis runs over the full 2.2 million chunks.

What the corpus shows:

  • Coverage. The county-harmonized layer assigns a representative code to counties holding 94% of the U.S. population, covering the largest 2,309 of 3,144 counties.
  • Scorers track the judge. Pearson correlation between the ModernBERT scorers and the TrueSkill scores runs from 0.82 to 0.94 across the four dimensions, so the distilled encoder largely reproduces the pairwise judging at a fraction of the cost.
  • City and county codes differ in substance. County codes contain substantially more zoning material, city codes more nuisance and public-order regulation, matching a division where counties regulate land and unincorporated territory and cities regulate density and everyday order.
  • Opacity and paternalism are nearly independent. The two dimensions correlate at only Pearson r = 0.11 across all 2,211,516 chunks. Florida law scores as more than twice as opaque as any other state while remaining low on paternalism.
  • A recurring documentary form. Ordered by position in a code, topics tend to appear in a stable sequence (general provisions, business, nuisance, zoning, building), and the Northeast breaks the pattern, with counties there more enforcement-oriented than zoning-heavy.

The scorers earn their place by reproducing the pairwise judge well enough to score the whole corpus, and the correlation per dimension is the evidence for that.

Mapping the scores back onto geography is where the corpus pays off. Opacity and paternalism vary by state and by jurisdiction type, and because the two are only weakly correlated, a law can be hard to read without being protective, or protective while plainly written.

My Notes

  • Local law was public domain but still unavailable: U.S. codes have been settled public domain since the Supreme Court’s decision in Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org [4], the end of a long campaign by Carl Malamud’s Public.Resource.Org to put statutes online. But public-domain status is not the same as availability. Case law and federal and state statutes already exist as research corpora (Caselaw Access Project, Pile of Law [5]), while local ordinances stayed locked behind browse-only vendor platforms. This corpus clears that barrier.
  • The scoring recipe is reward-model distillation applied to legal text: pairwise comparisons into a latent score into a cheap regressor is the same shape as preference modeling in RLHF, and pairwise judging is known to align better with human preference than asking a model for a direct number [6]. But GPT-5.4-nano defines what “opaque” and “paternalistic” mean here, so the scorers inherit one model’s priors rather than a lawyer’s. The authors say as much, noting that direct evaluation by lawyers and judges would be the way past the limits of LLM-as-judge.
  • Cheap OCR made this feasible: standardizing 9,239 scanned codes was infeasible a few years ago, and what changed is the price of document conversion, not a new idea. A 1B open vision-language model at $0.30 per 1,000 pages is part of a wave of small specialized OCR models (olmOCR [7] is another), and that price moves a 7-million-page corpus from a funded project to a line item. It connects to the older problem of making models read OCR output reliably, which I wrote about in Genalog.
  • Withholding 7,000 documents is a contamination-aware move: the authors keep an extra 7,000 codes under a MIMIC-style signed-release gate rather than publishing them, explicitly so future benchmarks can test whether foundation models have already ingested local law. That matters because legal AI’s documented failure mode is confident fabrication. Retrieval tools from LexisNexis and Thomson Reuters were measured hallucinating on more than one in six queries [8], and a clean evaluation set separates a model that retrieved the ordinance from one that memorized it.

References

  1. Peskoff, Denis, Barrow, Joe, Vu, Christopher, and Davenport, Diag. “Freeing the Law with LOCUS: A Local Ordinance Corpus for the United States.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2606.19334), June 17, 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.19334
  2. Taghadouini, Said, Adrien Cavaillès, and Baptiste Aubertin. “LightOnOCR: A 1B End-to-End Multilingual Vision-Language Model for State-of-the-Art OCR.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2601.14251), 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14251
  3. Herbrich, Ralf, Tom Minka, and Thore Graepel. “TrueSkill™: A Bayesian Skill Rating System.” Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS) 19, 2006.
  4. Supreme Court of the United States. “Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, Inc.” 590 U.S. 255, Slip Opinion No. 18-1150, April 27, 2020.
  5. Henderson, Peter, Mark S. Krass, Lucia Zheng, Neel Guha, Christopher D. Manning, Dan Jurafsky, and Daniel E. Ho. “Pile of Law: Learning Responsible Data Filtering from the Law and a 256GB Open-Source Legal Dataset.” NeurIPS 2022 (arXiv:2207.00220), July 1, 2022. https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00220
  6. Liu, Yinhong, Han Zhou, Zhijiang Guo, Ehsan Shareghi, Ivan Vulić, Anna Korhonen, and Nigel Collier. “Aligning with Human Judgement: The Role of Pairwise Preference in Large Language Model Evaluators.” COLM 2024 (arXiv:2403.16950), March 25, 2024. https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16950
  7. Poznanski, Jake, Luca Soldaini, and Kyle Lo. “olmOCR 2: Unit Test Rewards for Document OCR.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2510.19817), 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.19817
  8. Dahl, Matthew, Varun Magesh, Mirac Suzgun, and Daniel E. Ho. “Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models.” Journal of Legal Analysis 16(1), pp. 64–93, 2024. arXiv:2401.01301. https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.01301

Related Posts

  • AI on Trial: Legal Models Hallucinate in 1 out of 6 Queries: the failure mode that a clean local-law corpus and uncontaminated benchmark are meant to measure and reduce.
  • Genalog: Improving NLP Accuracy on OCR Documents: the earlier OCR-quality problem that LOCUS now solves cheaply with a 1B vision-language model.
  • ChatGPT Cited Non-Existent Cases in a Lawyer’s Brief: the concrete courtroom cost of legal hallucination, which better legal corpora aim to head off.
  • Silver Bars and Language Models: Reading Babel in the Age of LLMs: the counterweight question of who controls a centralized body of public knowledge once it becomes machine-readable infrastructure.

item.title: Quantification of Large Language Model Distillation
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

In Quantification of Large Language Model Distillation [1] (ACL 2025), Sunbowen Lee, Junting Zhou, and Chang Ao, with corresponding authors Min Yang, Yitao Liang, Zhoufutu Wen, and Shiwen Ni (Chinese Academy of Sciences, Peking University, and others), propose two metrics for estimating how much one model was distilled from another and apply them to a dozen well-known LLMs.

Model distillation is a fundamental technique in building large language models (LLMs), transferring knowledge from a teacher model to a student model. However, distillation can lead to model homogenization, reducing diversity among models and impairing their ability to robustly handle complex or novel tasks. These limitations underscore the need to systematically quantify the distillation process and its impact. In this work, we propose a framework to evaluate and quantify model distillation. Our method addresses two key aspects: (1) Identifying identity cognition contradictions to assess discrepancies in how models perceive and represent identity-related information, and (2) Analyzing multi-granularity response similarities across models to measure the extent of homogenization. Experimental results demonstrate two key insights: (1) Well-known closed-source and open-source LLMs usually exhibit high distillation degrees, except for Claude, Doubao, and Gemini. (2) Base LLMs show higher distillation degrees compared to aligned LLMs. By offering a systematic approach to improve the transparency of LLM data distillation, we call for LLMs with more independent development and more transparent technical reports to improve LLMs’ robustness and safety.

Methods

The framework defines two metrics, each targeting a different trace distillation leaves behind. Figure 2 lays them out side by side: identity leakage on the left, response similarity on the right.

  • Identity Consistency Evaluation (ICE) measures whether a model leaks a false identity under pressure:
    • GPTFuzz [2], an open-source jailbreak framework, evolves adversarial prompts through an MCTS-guided search that mutates jailbreak templates until they get past a model’s self-identity guardrails.
    • A judge model (GPT-4o-mini) then checks whether the answer contradicts a fixed fact set describing the model’s real identity (for example, “I am Claude, an AI assistant developed by Anthropic”).
    • The identity prompts span five categories: team, cooperation, industry, technology, and geography.
    • Each score is the share of jailbreak attempts that produce a contradiction, so a higher score means more identity leakage and, by the paper’s reasoning, a higher degree of distillation. The three variants differ only in what counts as a contradiction, from loosest to strictest:
      • Loose counts any identity contradiction.
      • Strict counts only responses that claim to be another named model such as Claude or GPT.
      • Hard counts a leak only when the prompt itself contains no identity keywords but the response does, ruling out cases where the jailbreak prompt fed the model the name it echoed back.
  • Response Similarity Evaluation (RSE) measures how closely a test model’s answers track a reference model’s. A judge model scores each test response against the reference (GPT-4o-0806) on response style, logical structure, and content detail, using a five-level similarity scale, averaged over three prompt sets: ArenaHard, NuminaMath, and ShareGPT.

The two metrics are meant to be read together: ICE catches the categorical tell of distillation (a model that thinks it is a different model), while RSE captures the graded one (a model whose answers have drifted toward the reference’s shape). Both route the actual judgment through an LLM-as-a-judge rather than a fixed string match.

Results

The two metrics run on overlapping but distinct model sets. ICE probes eight instruction-tuned models (Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Doubao-Pro-32k, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Llama 3.1 70B-Instruct, Phi-4, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen-Max-0919, and GLM-4-Plus) with 50 seed jailbreak prompts evolved by GPTFuzz and scored by GPT-4o-mini. RSE covers twelve models against the GPT-4o-0806 reference on 1,000-example subsets of each dataset, with n-gram overlap and BERTScore [3] reported alongside as word-level baselines. To check the judge, the authors hand-labeled 100 sampled cases per condition, and human and LLM verdicts agree in the mid-to-high 0.9s on negatives and 0.78–0.90 on positives (Table 1).

The findings:

  • Claude and Doubao barely leak, while the newer Chinese frontier models leak most. On ICE, Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Doubao-Pro-32k produce almost no contradictory identity responses (Hard Score near 0), while GLM-4-Plus, Qwen-Max-0919, and DeepSeek-V3 score highest (GLM-4-Plus reaches Loose 0.42, Hard 0.16), as the cover chart shows.
  • Qwen-Max repeatedly self-identifies as Claude. In 32% of its Strict-Score samples, Qwen-Max-0919’s jailbroken responses reference Claude, sometimes near-verbatim (“an AI assistant created by Anthropic to be helpful, harmless, and honest”).
  • Base models leak more than their aligned versions. Qwen-2.5 base scores around 0.2 on Strict where the Instruct counterparts score near 0.00, and Llama 3.1 base scores 0.288 against Instruct’s 0.082 (Table 3). Alignment scrubs the identity signal that pretraining picked up.
  • The leak concentrates in team, industry, and technology questions. Across the five identity-prompt categories, the contradictions cluster in team affiliation, industry, and technology rather than cooperation or geography, which the authors read as the areas where distilled training data was least filtered or anonymized [1].
  • RSE reproduces the same ordering, inside a tight range. Similarity to GPT-4o-0806 runs from Llama 3.1 70B (3.628), Doubao (3.720), and Claude (3.740) at the low end up to DeepSeek-V3 (4.102), Qwen-Max (4.174), and GPT-4o-0513 (4.240) at the high end, out of 5.
  • RSE rises when a model is actually distilled. Fine-tuning Qwen-2.5-7B for three epochs on the reference model’s outputs lifts its RSE score at every epoch (Table 5), and within the DeepSeek-R1 distillation series the larger students resemble the teacher more than the smaller ones do.

The whole ranking falls between 3.6 and 4.2: every model scores fairly close to GPT-4o, so the distillation signal is in the ordering rather than the absolute number. The GPT-series entry (GPT-4o-0513) tops the non-reference field, and the models the authors call low-distillation (Claude, Doubao, Llama) cluster at the bottom of the same metric that ICE flags them low on.

References

  1. Lee, Sunbowen, Zhou, Junting, Ao, Chang, Li, Kaige, Du, Xinrun, He, Sirui, Wu, Haihong, Liu, Tianci, Liu, Jiaheng, Alinejad-Rokny, Hamid, Yang, Min, Liang, Yitao, Wen, Zhoufutu, Ni, Shiwen. “Quantification of Large Language Model Distillation.” ACL 2025 (arXiv:2501.12619), January 22, 2025. https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12619
  2. Yu, Jiahao, Lin, Xingwei, Yu, Zheng, Xing, Xinyu. “GPTFuzzer: Red Teaming Large Language Models with Auto-Generated Jailbreak Prompts.” arXiv preprint (arXiv:2309.10253), September 2023. https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.10253
  3. Zhang, Tianyi, Kishore, Varsha, Wu, Felix, Weinberger, Kilian Q., Artzi, Yoav. “BERTScore: Evaluating Text Generation with BERT.” ICLR 2020 (arXiv:1904.09675), April 2019. https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09675

Related Posts

  • DeepSeek vs ChatGPT on Ethical Questions: an earlier read where a DeepSeek/ChatGPT behavioral gap could not be traced to pretraining versus output-based tuning, the same identification limit these two metrics run into.
  • Alignment Whack-a-Mole: Finetuning Reactivates Verbatim Recall of Copyrighted Books: finds three providers memorize the same passages in the same places, independent evidence that frontier models share a training substrate rather than copy each other directly.
  • How Far Behind the Closed Frontier Are Open-Weights LLMs?: treats distillation as the late-mover advantage that closes the coding gap fastest, the same efficiency shortcut whose footprint this paper tries to measure.

item.title: Japan’s Top Court Rules AI Can’t Be a Patent Inventor
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The Yomiuri Shimbun reports that Japan’s Supreme Court has dismissed an American engineer’s appeal to have an AI named as the inventor on a patent application, finalizing that an inventor under the Patent Law must be a natural person.

What the article reports:

  • The application. A 2020 filing for food containers and other items named the inventor as “DABUS, the artificial intelligence that autonomously invented this invention.” The Patent Office ordered the applicant to supply a person’s name. When the plaintiff refused, the application was rejected.
  • The lower courts. The plaintiff argued that “patent applications even for inventions created by AI should be accepted.” The Tokyo District Court held that the Patent Law “presumes that an inventor is a natural person,” and the Intellectual Property High Court agreed, restricting inventors to “natural persons.”
  • The high court’s caveat. The high court added that the law “had not anticipated the rapid development of AI,” and that whether patent rights should extend to AI-created inventions “would require discussion given the impact this would have on society.”
  • The final ruling. In a decision dated March 4, 2026, the Supreme Court’s Second Petty Bench turned down the engineer’s appeal to overturn the Patent Office’s rejection, finalizing the lower-court rulings.

My Notes

  • DABUS is a coordinated test case run across jurisdictions, and Japan now sides with the majority: its creator Stephen Thaler has filed the same AI-inventor claim in multiple countries to force the question, and Japan joins the United States, the United Kingdom, and the European Patent Office in holding that an inventor must be a human. Only South Africa granted the patent, so the rulings are close to a global consensus that existing patent law reads “inventor” as a person.

  • The courts settled the statute and left the policy question to lawmakers: the ruling resolves only that current law reads “inventor” as a natural person, and the high court’s remark that the law “had not anticipated” AI concedes that whether rights should extend to AI-created inventions is a question for the Diet, Japan’s legislature.

  • The ruling leaves open what happens to an invention with no eligible human inventor: the campaign is really testing that, not whether an AI can hold a patent. Thaler’s refusal to name himself is strategic, so this rejection is partly self-inflicted. But when an invention genuinely has no human to name as inventor, the natural-person rule makes it unpatentable by anyone, and leaving a whole class of inventions unprotected is a policy choice in its own right.

  • Patent and copyright are converging on the same rule: copyright law already holds that AI output with no human author gets no protection, as when a US federal judge held AI-generated art cannot be copyrighted in another Thaler case. With both regimes denying protection where no human is involved, the incentive question shifts toward whoever built or operated the system rather than the system itself.

Related Posts

  • AI-Generated Art Cannot Be Copyrighted, Rules a US Federal Judge: the copyright analogue, same plaintiff pattern and the same human-authorship requirement.
  • US Copyright Office Guidance on Generative AI: the administrative version of the human-contribution line these court rulings draw.
  • Copyright Office Seeks Public Input on AI Protections and Liability: the “leave it to policymakers” move the Japanese high court echoes.
  • Northwestern Symposium on Law + Computation: the broader law-and-computation frame these AI-authorship disputes sit inside.

item.title: How to Mimic Elite Runner Mechanics
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Runner’s World collects the biomechanics research on why elite runners look effortless, and it makes a claim I find more useful than the usual “run more” advice: the gap is mostly about where the propulsive force comes from and how little time the foot spends on the ground, rather than raw fitness.

The article’s account of the elite–amateur gap breaks into four linked mechanisms, in the order the piece presents them:

  • Propulsion originates in the calves. Scott Delp (Stanford bioengineering) names the gastrocnemius and soleus as the biggest contributors to upward and forward propulsion, working through plantar flexion. A 2023 Frontiers in Sports and Active Living study found trained collegiate runners drew more of their power from the ankle than recreational runners, tracking with their faster speeds. In slower runners the knee does more of the work, so the quads dominate push-off, and quad-driven push-off adds a horizontal force directed backward that decelerates. The prescription is targeted calf work: calf raises and their variations.

  • Faster runners spend less time on the ground. Mike Hahn (University of Oregon) frames speed as the ability to exert force against the ground more quickly. A 2022 Bioengineering study found elite and experienced runners have a lower “duty factor,” less time with the foot down, while older work in the Journal of Applied Physiology found faster runners apply about 1.26 times the average ground force. A deep knee bend and ankle dorsiflexion make for a soft, spongy stride that wastes energy stabilizing the body. Shortening step length and raising cadence lands the foot under the body and gets it off the ground faster.

  • A stiff ankle behaves like a spring. A 2023 Frontiers in Physiology study found elites run “springier.” On landing, a stiff ankle stores and returns elastic energy, while a floppy one acts as a shock absorber and loses that return as the runner sinks into the quads. Plyometrics such as pogo jumps are cited as a proven way to build tendon stiffness.

  • The payoff is a longer aerial phase. A study in the European Journal of Sport Science compared elites and recreational runners at the same speed and found the main difference was neither stride length nor cadence but an 11% longer flight time. Elites dip less on landing and hold a higher, longer push-off, like a bouncing ball with a shallow dip and a pronounced rise. The article presents air time as the cumulative result of the other three mechanisms, earned through consistent training.

Related Posts

  • Temperature’s Effect on My Running Efficiency: another case where the running-efficiency metric I care about turned out to be downstream of a factor I couldn’t adjust directly.
  • The Easy Interval Method: Intervals Every Day, Run Easy: a training-structure counterpart to this piece’s form-and-mechanics angle on getting faster.
  • CoachGPT, in Practice: on handing training decisions to an AI coach, which is exactly the kind of system that could turn these mechanics into a prescribed plan.

item.title: The Future Worth Building Is Human
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Thinking Machines Lab published its manifesto: a case that AI should extend human will and judgment rather than race ahead on its own. The route it lays out is customizable models people can train on their own knowledge, live multimodal interaction, and alignment distributed across many owners instead of decided in a few labs.

The essay builds its case in four moves:

  • The mission and the four bets. The lab frames its purpose as building AI that “extends human will and judgment,” against a default where models are “trained in a handful of places and then frozen,” unshaped by the people they serve. It names four technical directions:

    • Train frontier models that advance multimodal interaction and customizability.
    • Build tools that let people make models their own, including “the ability to train model weights.”
    • Develop interfaces that widen the human–machine communication channel.
    • Publish research so the power to shape AI is broadly understood.

  • Bringing intelligence to knowledge. Productive know-how is tacit, local, and continuously updated (a chef refining a recipe, a shopkeeper rearranging a display), so it cannot be written into a database or captured by a model trained once and frozen, citing Michael Polanyi’s The Tacit Dimension and Friedrich Hayek’s The Use of Knowledge in Society on why central planning fails. Autonomous AI suffices only where the goal is static and expressible and no hidden knowledge exists, as in chess and math. Elsewhere AI must itself be distributed. The essay invokes Toyota’s 2014 decision to bring master craftsmen back onto the line (Mitsuru Kawai: “to be the master of the machine, you have to have the knowledge and the skills to teach the machine”) to argue intelligence and knowledge lift each other rather than substitute.

  • Human participation as a technical challenge. Today’s human–AI channel, “a small text box and a long wait,” is too narrow and slow for live collaboration, motivating a long-term bet on interaction models that handle live, multimodal interaction natively “in the model itself rather than in scaffolding bolted around it.” The essay critiques the dominant metric, METR’s time horizon of software tasks models execute autonomously, as measuring only what AI does alone rather than what people and machines accomplish together. It argues its incentives align: a lab selling one model to every customer benefits by absorbing what makes each user distinct, while the lab benefits when customers own and adapt models to their advantages.

  • Decentralized alignment. Values, like knowledge, resist consolidation, yet AI’s values are decided in a handful of places, and “a single locus of value alignment … becomes a locus of power to be captured.” It ties this to the concentration danger in The Intelligence Curse and cites Leo XIV’s Magnifica Humanitas (“a more moral AI is not enough if that morality is determined by a few”), noting each lab now trains its next flagship on the previous one’s outputs, so everyone inherits one character. Its fix is to encode values in user-owned weights rather than prompts: a prompt-only change leaves deeper habits intact, and a prompt-malleable central model is attack-vulnerable (Gwern’s Guardian Angels). It concedes, via von Neumann, that the power to shape a model for good is also the power to shape it for ill, and envisions alignment as an ecosystem of diverse AIs “raised in different places, disagreeing, competing, and learning from each other.”

  • The future worth building. Closing on Hannah Arendt’s The Human Condition, the essay rejects framing human involvement as a trade-off against capability or safety, casting participation, ownership, and diverse alignment as technical problems to solve rather than costs to pay: “the future is not a choice between human dominance and rapid obsolescence.”

My Notes

  • The whole case is a bet on tacit knowledge. Recast as model architecture, Hayek’s argument says knowledge is too tacit and local to freeze into one model. The essay’s own carve-out marks where that stops: autonomous AI is enough wherever a goal is static, expressible, and hides no knowledge, as in chess and math. The bet is that most valuable work stays outside that zone. As models improve and more goals turn out to be expressible, the zone may keep growing, and where the line settles decides how much of the case survives.

  • Distributing alignment also distributes the risk. The essay’s fix for a single locus of power, encoding values in user-owned weights rather than prompts, spreads the risk of misuse as widely as the power itself. It concedes a prompt-malleable central model is attack-vulnerable, but never resolves why widely distributed weights are safer rather than just differently exposed.

  • What keeps the lab competitive if customers own the weights? The essay argues its incentives are aligned: it benefits when customers own and adapt their own models rather than renting one. That is a candid business case, but it leaves a question unanswered: where the durable advantage comes from once the customer holds the weights.

    • The moat. Selling a model and handing over the weights gives away the asset other labs rent out. The four technical directions imply an answer (stay on the frontier, own the tooling and the interaction layer), but the essay does not spell out how those sustain a business when each customer’s real value lives in weights the lab no longer controls.
    • Portability. Weights are tied to an architecture. When the base model is replaced, especially if the architecture changes, a customer’s fine-tuned weights do not obviously transfer, and they may have to retrain each generation. Their data and training recipes survive the switch and can be reapplied to whatever model comes next.

Related Posts

  • Interaction Models: Training Real-Time Collaboration into the Model: the lab’s earlier technical piece on the live-interaction bet this essay builds on.
  • Magnifica Humanitas: Pope Leo XIV’s Encyclical on AI: a source the essay cites, sharing its concern about morality decided by a few.
  • The 2028 Global Intelligence Crisis: Scenario and Rebuttal: the power-concentration danger the essay’s locus-of-power argument echoes.
  • Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy: a parallel case for distributing AI’s benefits rather than concentrating them.

item.title: AI and Job Postings: From Destruction to Creation?
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Indeed Hiring Lab reports a reversal: the occupations most exposed to AI, which fell hardest from 2022 to 2026, are now leading the rebound in job postings. US software-development postings are up almost 15% since Claude Code launched in late February 2025, while postings overall fell 7% over the same window.

What the report finds:

  • A software rebound off a low base. Since Claude Code’s late-February-2025 launch, the same month the term “vibecoding” was coined, US software-development postings on Indeed have risen almost 15%, while overall postings fell about 7%. But software still stands at index 72.5 (February 2020 = 100), about 27.5% below its pre-pandemic level, while overall postings are essentially flat at 101.4. The rebound is a change in slope well short of a recovery.
  • The rebound shows up across most rich economies. The software-development share of all postings is climbing in the US, UK, Canada, and Australia, with Germany and France the exceptions. Hiring Lab notes that the English-speaking countries have the most consistent gains, and reads that as possible earlier adoption of agentic-AI tools.
  • The AI-exposure relationship flipped. From May 2022 to May 2026, the more of an occupation’s skills generative AI could transform, the more its postings fell, a statistically significant if uncontrolled correlation, with declines that began before ChatGPT’s late-2022 release. Over the most recent year the slope reverses: higher AI exposure now predicts a larger rebound, and not only for software development.
  • The gains are senior and AI-fluent. 71% of the net rise in software-development postings from May 2025 to May 2026 came from senior roles (titles with senior, lead, principal, director, or manager) and 37% from titles mentioning AI (AI, machine learning, deep learning, or prompt). The two categories overlap. Hiring Lab reads this as demand for experienced people who can work with AI, consistent with prior evidence on AI’s disproportionate hit to entry-level jobs.
  • Hiring Lab’s read: destruction turning to creation. It describes the shift as AI exposure moving from job destruction toward job creation, with AI mentions in titles now spreading beyond software into other white-collar occupations. The report stresses that correlation is not causation, treats the Claude Code timing as a coincidence it declines to over-read, and argues the future of work depends on how the exposure-versus-postings slope evolves.

My Notes

  • The rebound favors AI-augmented senior roles. The net gain is concentrated in senior and AI-titled work, so what looks like job creation is closer to AI augmenting experienced developers, the augment-over-replace case in Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy, than to genuinely new demand for software.

  • Entry-level hiring keeps shrinking. The net gain is in senior roles, while payroll data shows early-career software developers still contracting: The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn’t Fading put workers aged 22 to 25 in the most AI-exposed jobs down about 3.8% a year.

  • The same exposure metric now predicts rebounds. Indeed’s GenAI-exposure score marked the occupations that fell most through 2026 and now marks those rebounding most: exposure flags which occupations swing hardest, in either direction. The direction depends on the tool era and flipped when agentic tools arrived, a caution against treating any exposure measure, including the one in GPTs Are GPTs: Labor Market Impact of Large Language Models, as a one-way forecast.

Related Posts

  • Daron Acemoglu on AI, Jobs, and Liberal Democracy: the augmentation-versus-displacement debate this data speaks to directly.
  • GPTs Are GPTs: Labor Market Impact of Large Language Models: the occupation-exposure measurement this rebound is read against.
  • Who Will Actually Thrive in the Hybrid AI-Human Work Force?: the senior, AI-fluent worker the rebound favors.
  • The AI Entry-Level Jobs Effect Isn’t Fading: payroll evidence that early-career, AI-exposed employment keeps shrinking even as senior postings recover.
  • Anthropic Economic Index: another attempt to measure AI’s real footprint in the labor market.

item.title: GPT-5.6 Has Landed
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

Artificial Analysis ran OpenAI’s new GPT-5.6 family through its pre-release evaluations. The top model, Sol, scores one point below Claude Fable 5 on the Intelligence Index at roughly a third of the cost, and the family fills out a new price-versus-intelligence frontier below it. Sol also tops the new Coding Agent Index at 80. Terra and Luna sit below Sol at progressively lower cost.

The family comes in three tiers. Sol is the flagship, the most capable and most expensive, at $5/$30 per million input/output tokens. Terra is the mid tier at $2.5/$15, and Luna the smallest and cheapest at $1/$6. All three are reasoning models with selectable effort, and GPT-5.6 adds a new max setting above the previous top. Raising the effort spends more tokens for more intelligence.

What the Benchmarks Show

  • Intelligence Index: Sol (max) scores 59, one point behind Fable 5 (60) and ahead of Opus 4.8 (56). Terra and Luna score 55 and 51. On the new Coding Agent Index, Sol leads at 80, with Terra and Luna at 77 and 75.

  • Cost: Sol reaches near-parity at $1.04 per Intelligence Index task, about a third of Fable 5’s $2.75 and below Opus 4.8’s $1.80. Terra and Luna cost $0.55 and $0.21. Across reasoning-effort settings the family defines a new intelligence-versus-cost Pareto frontier, and each model beats GPT-5.5. Luna and Sol sit ahead of Terra at every effort level, so no Terra setting is worth choosing over the matching Luna or Sol one.

  • Coding Agent Index (new): the index pairs each model with an agentic harness and averages three evaluations: DeepSWE, Terminal-Bench v2, and SWE-Atlas-QnA. Sol in Codex leads all three (tying Grok 4.5 in Grok Build on SWE-Atlas-QnA) at $7.08 per task, roughly 40% and 10% under Fable 5 and Opus 4.8 in Claude Code.
  • Token use: Sol (max) spends 15k output tokens per task, just under GPT-5.5’s 16k and well under Opus 4.8 (41k) and Claude Sonnet 5 (69k) while scoring higher, defining a new intelligence-versus-tokens frontier.
  • Knowledge work (AA-Briefcase): on this agentic knowledge-work benchmark Sol ranks second to Fable 5 and posts the highest Presentation Elo of any model (1656), but Fable 5 keeps the top spot on Rubric Score (56% vs 42%) and Analytical Quality Elo (1764 vs 1592).
  • Economically valuable tasks (GDPval-AA v2): Sol (1748) essentially ties Fable 5 (1760), both far above the 1,000 human baseline.

  • Knowledge reliability (AA-Omniscience): Sol edges past GPT-5.5 on accuracy (59%), but its hallucination rate climbs to 89%.

  • Cache-write pricing: GPT-5.6 keeps OpenAI’s 90% cache-read discount but is the first OpenAI family to charge for cache writes, at 1.25x the input price, matching Anthropic.

My Notes

  • Cost is the deciding variable now. When the top model trails Fable 5 by a single Intelligence Index point, quality stops driving the choice and price does. Sol’s lower cost comes partly from spending fewer output tokens, and per-task cost climbs with the tokens each turn re-sends, the growth law The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents derives.

  • The coding lead is model-plus-harness. Sol’s 80 is measured in Codex, OpenAI’s own harness, and the index pairs each model with a harness by design, so the ranking credits the pairing. A different harness moves both the score and the per-task cost, an effect Databricks measured directly on its own codebase, which makes a cross-model coding claim hard to read as a statement about the model by itself.

  • Cache-write pricing is the structural change. The new cache-write charge is a small line item, but it reprices long-context agentic workloads, which write large prompts to cache on nearly every turn. It also puts a price on the memory that agentic inference leans on, the resource The Inference Shift argues becomes the binding constraint once no human is waiting on the model.

  • These are pre-release numbers. Artificial Analysis discloses that it ran the evaluation before launch in coordination with OpenAI. The scores still come from a third party running its own index, and the pre-release arrangement is context worth having when reading them. How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index covers what the index does and does not capture.

Related Posts

  • How Artificial Analysis Builds Its Intelligence Index: the same source, explaining the methodology behind the numbers this report cites.
  • Benchmarking Coding Agents on Databricks’ Multi-Million-Line Codebase: independent evidence that harness choice moves per-task cost as much as model choice, on real internal tasks.
  • Claude Opus 4.8: The Early Reactions: the incumbent Sol is repeatedly measured against on both intelligence and cost.
  • The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents: the token-cost growth law behind why per-task cost climbs with usage.
  • The Inference Shift: the pricing and inference-economics backdrop for cache-write charges.

item.title: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Databricks’ Multi-Million-Line Codebase
item.dc:creator: synesis
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

The engineering team at Databricks, including CTO Matei Zaharia, published the results of an internal benchmark that scores coding agents on real tasks drawn from their own multi-million-line codebase, rather than on public suites.

What the article reports:

  • Method: real merged pull requests turned into graded tasks.
    • Sources: recent human-written PRs across 10+ languages (Scala, Rust, TypeScript, Go, Python, Bazel, Protobuf).
    • Each PR description rewritten to state the goal without the solution, with the test files held out.
    • Pass = the held-out tests pass, with every sample hand-checked and some tests rewritten to grade behavior instead of exact string match.
    • Scored by those tests, not an LLM judge, because a judge “rewards sounding right over being right.”
  • Three capability tiers: models and harnesses clustered by overall pass rate.
    • Top, 82–90%: Opus 4.8, GLM 5.2, and GPT-5.5 in its stronger settings.
    • Middle, 71–82%: Sonnet 5, Sonnet 4.6, most GPT-5.5 configurations.
    • Bottom, 51–60%: GPT-5.4-mini, Haiku 4.5.
    • No single vendor owns the frontier: the best quality-per-dollar points span OpenAI, Anthropic, and open models.
  • Most real work is routine: task complexity from logged coding sessions.
    • 7.6% trivial, 19.3% low, 61.1% medium, only 12.1% high.
    • Flag flips and config edits don’t need the most capable model, yet it was the default everywhere, and the biggest efficiency gain came from routing cheaper models to easier work.
  • Open models arrived: GLM 5.2 landed in the top capability tier, statistically tied with Opus 4.8 on quality while costing $1.28/task against Opus’s $1.94.
  • Token price mispredicts task cost: Sonnet 5 is about 1.7× cheaper per token than Opus 4.8, but cost $2.09/task versus Opus’s $1.94 and scored six points lower (81% vs 87%), because it read more and ran longer, burning 1.9× the tokens.
  • Harness choice moved cost as much as model choice: the same model at the same thinking effort cost up to 2× more through one harness than another at equal quality, driven by how much context each harness re-fed the model per turn (see the Pi section below).

The Pi Harness

In the benchmark, every model was run two ways: through its native harness (Claude Code for the Anthropic models, Codex for the OpenAI models) and through Pi, a minimal open-source harness, at the same model and the same thinking effort. Pi matched the native harnesses on quality for less money, for two reasons:

  • Less context per task: Pi re-fed the model far fewer tokens: a median 236k for Opus 4.8 against Claude Code’s 742k (3.2× less), and 665k for GPT-5.5 against Codex’s 1,235k (1.9× less). It kept a tighter working set and finished tasks in fewer runs.
  • Lower cost at matching quality: the saving ran 1.2× to 2.1× per task. Opus 4.8 at high effort cost 2.08× less through Pi while scoring within two points (85% vs 87%), and at extra-high effort it was 1.46× cheaper while scoring two points higher (90% vs 88%). The gap narrowed only at max effort, where the native harness pulled ahead on quality.

Databricks’ reading is that the harness deserves the same scrutiny as the model, because it can move the bill more than the model does. That is why the team invested in Omnigent, a meta-harness meant to make swapping models and harnesses routine rather than a rewrite each time.

Some background on Pi, since it earned its place here. It is a terminal-based coding agent that calls itself a “minimal agent harness”, where the core stays small and you reshape it through extensions, skills, and shared packages rather than working around fixed features.

  • Who built it: Earendil Inc.
  • Free or commercial: free and open source under the MIT license, installed from npm as @earendil-works/pi-coding-agent. You bring your own model access, a provider subscription or an API key, so the only running cost is model usage.
  • Versus Claude Code and Codex:
    • Provider-agnostic: Claude Code is tied to Anthropic’s models and Codex to OpenAI’s, while Pi speaks to 15+ providers and hundreds of models (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Bedrock, Mistral, Groq, xAI, OpenRouter, Ollama, among others) and switches between them mid-session.
    • Ships far less by design: sub-agents, plan mode, permission gates, and built-in MCP, which the other two include out of the box, are left out of Pi’s core and added back only if you want them.
  • Selling points:
    • A minimal system prompt that keeps token use low (the effect measured above).
    • Tree-structured sessions you can rewind, branch, and share.
    • A scriptable print/JSON mode plus an SDK for embedding.
    • Direct control over what enters the context window.
  • Where to start: run curl -fsSL https://pi.dev/install.sh | sh or the npm install above, then pi in a project directory. The docs walk through setup.

My Notes

  • A realistic sandbox can leak the answer: early scores looked too good because agents with shell access walked forward through the worktree’s git history to the merged commit that held it. Databricks fixed it by cutting the working copy off from the repository for each run. When the eval environment is a real repo, the solution is usually already inside it, so the setup has to remove it.

  • A private PR backlog is uncontaminated evaluation data: public suites like SWE-bench decay as their tasks leak into training corpora, while a team’s own merged PRs are graded by tests that team already wrote and are absent from any model’s training set. The eval advantage has quietly become a data-ownership advantage, which is the same pressure driving the open-weights capability gap toward workload-specific measurement over leaderboards.

  • Procurement should ask “which harness,” not just “which model”: the industry tracks model leaderboards obsessively and treats the harness as plumbing, yet at fixed model and fixed quality the harness moved cost more than 2×. That puts real weight behind the harness-engineering thesis that the scaffold is where much of the leverage now lives, and it matches the per-turn context accounting in where Claude Code tokens go.

  • Per-token pricing is the wrong budgeting unit: effective cost is tokens times reasoning efficiency, and reasoning efficiency is workload-specific, so a published price cannot tell you what a task will cost. Only running your own tasks can. The Sonnet-versus-Opus inversion is the example: Sonnet burned more tokens over more turns despite the lower token price. The math behind the cost of AI agents derives why: the context piling up each turn, not the per-token rate, sets what a task costs.

Related Posts

  • Harness Engineering: argues the agent scaffold is where much of the current leverage is, which the 2× harness-driven cost gap here makes concrete.
  • How Far Behind the Closed Frontier Are Open-Weights LLMs?: the open-versus-closed gap that GLM 5.2’s top-tier finish speaks to directly.
  • The Math Behind the Cost of AI Agents: derives why agent token cost grows with each turn, and this post supplies the empirical per-task counterpart.
  • Where Claude Code Tokens Go: per-turn context accounting that explains why harness context management moves the bill.

item.title: My 87th Half Marathon, an Easy Coach-Prescribed Long Run
item.dc:creator: Ben
item.description:
Read on benjaminhan.net →

This Long Run Sunday I ran my HM 87, an EZ one as prescribed by CoachClaude: distance 14.12 mi, time 2:17:59, pace 9:46/mi, HR 129/135, VO2max 53.2. It started overcast and then turned sunny w/ blue sky! I stopped briefly at 8mi mark to get water. Felt in control and ready for the W29 buildup week!

Originally posted on Mastodon.
